comments.author: @ask291s
comments.text:
The Chinese mainland has historically been a region where Han and non-Han peoples fought struggles for survival and dominance. The first period in which China came under the rule of a non-Han people was during the Sui dynasty. This make Japan to believe that if even a non-Han ruler could claim the title of Emperor, then Japan could also claim the title of the Emperor of the East and stand on equal footing with China. This became a famous historical episode.

Later, the Song dynasty restored Han rule. It was a truly glorious period in Chinese history, when science and technology reached their greatest heights. But after that, the ruling power shifted repeatedly the non-Han Yuan dynasty, the Han Ming dynasty, and then the non-Han Qing dynasty. With each change in the ruling regime, China gradually lost some of the brilliance it had once possessed, despite the military strength of these dynasties.

Meanwhile, Japan was never subjected to foreign rule. It independently developed practices such as futures trading and traditional wasan mathematics, while also accumulating European knowledge through the Dutch. This gave Japan certain advantages in adapting to Western culture compared with other Asian countries.

The term "China"—in its original linguistic sense—signifies the "Central Empire." Throughout thousands of years of history, it has consistently served as the epicenter of East Asian order and culture. Japan, conversely, has historically functioned as a Confucian-militaristic societal bloc—and, as such, stands as a cultural byproduct of the Chinese civilization. Following the Meiji Restoration, the Japanese people endeavored to cast off the "barbaric" tenets of Confucianism; however, due to their steadfast rejection of Christianity, Japan remains—to this very day—a quintessential Confucian society. In the dominant historical narrative of the Chinese people, Japan has never been regarded as a major power—it was considered inferior even to Korea, ranking roughly on par with Myanmar. However, in a Confucian society where merit is measured by strength, Japan—following the accession of Emperor Meiji—rapidly transformed itself into East Asia's sole modernized industrial nation by adopting Western technology and the Prussian political system. Subsequently, Japan turned against China; the "Century of Humiliation at the Hands of Japan"—a phrase commonly used by the Chinese—refers precisely to this period.
All Confucian societies adhere to the "jungle law" wherein "the victor becomes king, while the vanquished is branded a bandit." Their social structure resembles that of a beehive or an anthill: every member functions merely as a cog within the state apparatus—willing to sacrifice themselves and resort to any means necessary to achieve a singular, collective objective—thereby ultimately fulfilling the aims of the state. Consequently, in this world, apart from white Christian nations, only Confucian societies have proven capable of emerging as developed industrial powers.

For the past century or so, Japan has successfully exploited the lag in China's political reforms to completely suppress China. However, once China also industrializes, Japan will have no chance; the vast difference in size between the two countries places them on entirely different levels.
